content: In France, the national social security system ensures that prenatal and postnatal care are entirely free of charge at public hospitals. Working women are eligible for 16 weeks of paid maternity leave, receiving between €9.29 ($10.94) and €84.90 ($100) daily, depending on previous earnings. During pregnancy and the time surrounding birth, financial strain is comparable to that of other periods: low-income families continue to face challenges, but their situation does not worsen significantly, while families with more resources remain comfortable. Despite this, there is little direct support for new mothers. Fathers are only entitled to 11 days of leave, which is insufficient for a mother to properly recover after giving birth. As a result, new mothers must handle the relentless responsibilities of caring for their infant while also working on their own recovery. Finding childcare is another obstacle, especially in areas like Paris, where public childcare programs fall short of demand. Costs of care can vary significantly; in state-run crèches, the lowest-income families might pay around €1,000 ($1,177.59) annually, but available spots are very limited—about one for every eight children. Therefore, many families must turn to private options such as nannies or home-based care. Any other questions?
